\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:returnbound}
\emph{The identity is the likeliest place.} Let $X$ be a symmetric random walk on a finite group $G$, started at the identity $e$,
and write $p_t(g)=P(X_t=g)$. This means $X_0=e$ and $X_t=\xi_1\cdots\xi_t$, where the increments are independent, all have the same distribution $\mu$, and $\mu(g)=\mu(g^{-1})$. Times $t$ are nonnegative integers; all probabilities here concern finite experiments.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $p_{2t}(e)=\sum_{g}p_t(g)^2$, and deduce that $p_{2t}(g)\le p_{2t}(e)$ for every $g\in G$ and that $p_{2t}(e)\ge\frac1{|G|}$.
\item Show that $t\mapsto p_{2t}(e)$ is non-increasing.
\item Show that $p_{2t+1}(e)$ can be $0$ for every $t$, but that $p_{2t+1}(g)\le p_{2t}(e)$ for all $g$ and $t$.
\item For $n\ge1$, the walk on $\Z/n\Z$ with equally likely steps $\pm1$, started at $0$, is at time $2t$ at $0$ with probability $\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos^{2t}\frac{2\pi k}n$. Derive this from the finite geometric sum for roots of unity, then check (a) and
(b) directly on this formula.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

entries.hypotheses_domain:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:sieving}
\emph{Cyclic sieving.} Let $n\ge1$ and $[m]_q=1+q+\dots+q^{m-1}$, $[m]_q!=[1]_q[2]_q\cdots[m]_q$, and for $0\le k\le n$
\[
\qbinom nk=\frac{[n]_q!}{[k]_q!\,[n-k]_q!},\qquad [0]_q!=1.
\]
Set $\qbinom nk=0$ for $k<0$ or $k>n$; this supplies the boundary terms of the recurrence.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $\qbinom nk=\qbinom{n-1}{k-1}+q^k\qbinom{n-1}k$, and deduce that $\qbinom nk$ is a polynomial in $q$ with
non-negative integer coefficients.
\item Let $m\mid n$ and let $\zeta$ be a primitive $m$-th root of unity. Show that the value of this polynomial at $\zeta$
is $\binom{n/m}{k/m}$ if $m\mid k$, and $0$ otherwise.
\item The rotation $g:x\mapsto x+1$ of $\Z/n\Z$ acts on the $k$-element subsets of $\Z/n\Z$. Show that for every $j$, the
number of subsets fixed by $g^j$ is the value of $\qbinom nk$ at $q=e^{2i\pi j/n}$.
\item Deduce the number of necklaces with $n$ beads, $k$ of them black, up to rotation, and check that there are $4$ for
$n=6$, $k=3$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

entries.hypotheses_domain:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{pb:flags}
\emph{Flags and the field with one element.} Let $V=\mathbb F_q^n$ and $[m]_q=1+q+\dots+q^{m-1}$, $[n]_q!=[1]_q[2]_q\cdots[n]_q$.
A \emph{complete flag} is a chain $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\dots\subset V_n=V$ with $\dim V_i=i$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $V$ has $[n]_q!$ complete flags.
\item Let $U$ be a subspace of dimension $k$. Show that $U$ has exactly $q^{k(n-k)}$ complements $W$ (subspaces with $U\oplus W=V$).
\item Show that $|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=q^{\binom n2}(q-1)^n\,[n]_q!$, by letting $GL_n$ act on flags.
\item Set $q=1$ in the formulas of (a) and (b). What do flags and complements become, and what does (c) say about the
symmetric group?
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:discphi}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $\zeta=e^{2i\pi/p}$ and $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that the discriminant $\prod_{1\le i<j\le p-1}(\zeta^i-\zeta^j)^2$ of $\Phi_p$ equals $(p^*)\,p^{p-3}$, and
deduce that $\sqrt{p^*}\in\Q(\zeta)$.
\item (Zolotarev) For $a$ prime to $p$, let $\pi_a$ be the permutation $x\mapsto ax$ of $\Z/p\Z$. Show that the sign of
$\pi_a$ is the Legendre symbol $\bigl(\frac ap\bigr)$.
\item Let $\sigma_a$ be the automorphism of $\Q(\zeta)$ with $\sigma_a(\zeta)=\zeta^a$. Show that
$\sigma_a(\sqrt{p^*})=\bigl(\frac ap\bigr)\sqrt{p^*}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

entries.hypotheses_domain:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{ex:primitive}
\emph{Finding a primitive element, and a boundary in positive characteristic.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item In Theorem~\ref{thm:primitiveelement}, let the minimal polynomials of
$\alpha,\beta$ have degrees $m,n$. Show that one of the integers
$c\in\{0,1,\ldots,m(n-1)\}$ satisfies $K(\alpha,\beta)=K(\alpha+c\beta)$.
\item Over $K=\mathbb Q$, show that every nonzero rational $c$ works for
$\alpha=\sqrt2$, $\beta=\sqrt3$. Recover both square roots explicitly from
$\gamma=\sqrt2+c\sqrt3$.
\item Let $p$ be prime, $S,T$ independent formal indeterminates,
$L=\mathbb F_p(S,T)=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb F_p[S,T])$ and
$K=\mathbb F_p(S^p,T^p)\subseteq L$. Prove that the $p^2$ monomials
$S^iT^j$, $0\le i,j<p$, form a $K$-basis of $L$, while every
$\gamma\in L$ satisfies $\gamma^p\in K$. Deduce that $L/K$ has no
primitive element.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:moore}
\emph{The Moore determinant.} Let $q$ be a prime power, $n\ge0$, $m\ge1$, and $\Delta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\det\bigl(x_i^{q^{j-1}}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le n}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item (Moore, 1896.) Show that
\[
\Delta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\ \prod_{c\in\mathbb F_q^{i-1}}\bigl(x_i+c_1x_1+\dots+c_{i-1}x_{i-1}\bigr)
\]
in $\mathbb F_q[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.
\item Deduce that $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in\mathbb F_{q^m}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb F_q$ if and only if
$\Delta(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)\ne0$.
\item Let $V\subset\mathbb F_{q^m}$ be an $\mathbb F_q$-subspace. Show that $P_V(X)=\prod_{v\in V}(X-v)$ is a linear combination
of $X,X^q,X^{q^2},\dots$, so that $P_V(x+y)=P_V(x)+P_V(y)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{pb:mseq}
\emph{Maximal length sequences.} Let $n\ge1$ and let $\alpha$ generate the cyclic group $\mathbb F_{2^n}^*$, $f=X^n+c_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\dots+c_0$ its
minimal polynomial over $\mathbb F_2$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\beta^{2^j}$, and
$s_k=\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^k)\in\mathbb F_2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $s_{k+n}=c_{n-1}s_{k+n-1}+\dots+c_0s_k$ for all $k$.
\item Show that the map $\beta\mapsto\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}(\beta),\operatorname{Tr}(\beta\alpha),\dots,\operatorname{Tr}(\beta\alpha^{n-1})\bigr)$ is a bijection
$\mathbb F_{2^n}\to\mathbb F_2^n$. Deduce that $(s_k)$ has period $2^n-1$, that every non-zero block of $n$ bits appears exactly
once among the windows $(s_k,\dots,s_{k+n-1})$, $0\le k<2^n-1$, and that every non-zero sequence satisfying the recurrence of (a)
is a shift of $(s_k)$.
\item Show that a period contains $2^{n-1}$ ones and $2^{n-1}-1$ zeros, and that for $0<t<2^n-1$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-2}(-1)^{s_k+s_{k+t}}=-1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

minimal polynomial over $\mathbb F_2$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\beta^{2^j}$, and
$s_k=\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^k)\in\mathbb F_2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $s_{k+n}=c_{n-1}s_{k+n-1}+\dots+c_0s_k$ for all $k$.
\item Show that the map $\beta\mapsto\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}(\beta),\operatorname{Tr}(\beta\alpha),\dots,\operatorname{Tr}(\beta\alpha^{n-1})\bigr)$ is a bijection
$\mathbb F_{2^n}\to\mathbb F_2^n$. Deduce that $(s_k)$ has period $2^n-1$, that every non-zero block of $n$ bits appears exactly
once among the windows $(s_k,\dots,s_{k+n-1})$, $0\le k<2^n-1$, and that every non-zero sequence satisfying the recurrence of (a)
is a shift of $(s_k)$.
\item Show that a period contains $2^{n-1}$ ones and $2^{n-1}-1$ zeros, and that for $0<t<2^n-1$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-2}(-1)^{s_k+s_{k+t}}=-1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

Standing scope: finite G, finite complex dimension; irreducible means nonzero. \begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:frobschur}
Let $G$ be finite, $r(g)$ the number of $x\in G$ with $x^2=g$, and for an irreducible character $\chi$ let
$\nu(\chi)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{x\in G}\chi(x^2)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that $\nu(\chi)\in\{-1,0,1\}$, and that $\nu(\chi)\ne0$ if and only if $\chi$ is real-valued.
\item (Frobenius and Schur, 1906.) Show that $r=\sum_\chi\nu(\chi)\chi$.
\item Show that $\nu=-1$ for the irreducible character of degree $2$ of the quaternion group $Q_8$.
\item Show that $\nu(\chi)=1$ when the representation can be realised by real matrices. Prove the converse as well: an irreducible representation with $\nu=1$ can be realised by real matrices.
\item For $n\ge0$ (with $\mathfrak S_0$ the trivial permutation group), let
$\mathcal I_n=\{\tau\in\mathfrak S_n:\tau^2=e\}$.
On a real space with basis $(v_\tau)_{\tau\in\mathcal I_n}$ define
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\pi)v_\tau&=(-1)^{N(\pi,\tau)}v_{\pi\tau\pi^{-1}},\\
N(\pi,\tau)&=\#\{1\le a<b\le n:\tau(a)=b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Show that this is a representation and that its character at $\pi$ counts
$x\in\mathfrak S_n$ with $x^2=\pi$.
Deduce that every irreducible representation of $\mathfrak S_n$ can be
realised by real matrices, and that the sum of its irreducible degrees is
$\#\{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_n:\sigma^2=e\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

entries.claim:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:jensen}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that for real $x$ and $\theta$ and $n\ge1$,
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(x^2-2x\cos\Bigl(\theta+\frac{2\pi k}n\Bigr)+1\Bigr)=x^{2n}-2x^n\cos n\theta+1.
\]
\item Deduce Poisson's integral: for $|x|\ne1$, $\int_0^\pi\log(1-2x\cos\theta+x^2)\dd\theta$ is $0$ if $|x|<1$ and
$2\pi\log|x|$ if $|x|>1$.
\item Let $P=a\prod_{k=1}^d(X-z_k)\in\C[X]$, $a\ne0$, with no root of modulus $1$. Show that
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log\bigl|P(e^{i\theta})\bigr|\dd\theta=\log|a|+\sum_{k=1}^d\log\max(1,|z_k|).
\]
What does Problem~\ref{pb:kronecker} say about the polynomials of $\Z[X]$ for which this is $0$?
\item Extend the formula to roots on the unit circle, interpreting the integral as an improper limit at the finitely many zero angles. Characterize the integer polynomials with zero mean in this extended case.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

entries.initial_reconstruction_record:
Product factors into nth-root polynomials and their conjugates,
giving x^(2n)−2x^n cos(n theta)+1. At theta0 take log/n: mean of
log(1−2xcos(2pi k/n)+x²) equals2log|1−x^n|/n, tends0 for|x|<1 and
2log|x| for|x|>1. To turn this into the integral, locally construct the needed
Riemann integrals for Lipschitz functions: common refinements bound sum error by
M times interval-length times mesh, so sums Cauchy and same limit for all tags.
Derivative of this log function is uniformly bounded because denominator>=
(|x|−1)²>0; MVT supplies Lipschitz. This earns this particular integral without
future V7 analysis. Symmetry halves the2pi integral. Each factor e^itheta−z
is a translate of a radial factor; translation invariance follows by shifted
partitions for periodic Lipschitz functions. Half-log gives logmax(1,|z|), finite
linearity gives Jensen. For integer P with no unit-circle root, zero mean forces
leading coefficient±1 and all roots modulus<1; strip zero roots and use actual
Kronecker to conclude P=±X^r. Without the no-unit-circle restriction, discussing
cyclotomic factors would also require earning integrable log singularities;
do not silently include that extension. Three stars because local analysis is needed.

entries.claim:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:dodecaturns}
\emph{Random turns of an icosahedron.} The rotation group of the regular icosahedron is isomorphic to $A_5$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteso3}), and the
$20$ rotations by a third of a turn about the axes through the centres of opposite faces form the conjugacy class of the
$3$-cycles. An icosahedron is turned, again and again, by a uniformly chosen one of these $20$ rotations.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $\mu$ be a probability on a finite group $G$ that is constant on conjugacy classes, and $\mu^{*t}$ the law of the walk at integer time
$t\ge0$, started at $e$. Show that, for every $g\in G$,
\[
\mu^{*t}(g)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_\chi\chi(1)\overline{\chi(g)}\,\Bigl(\frac{\hat\mu(\chi)}{\chi(1)}\Bigr)^t,\qquad\hat\mu(\chi)=\sum_{h\in G}\mu(h)\chi(h),
\]
the sum being over the irreducible characters of $G$. At $t=0$ interpret every scalar's zeroth power as $1$, including $0^0$, because it comes from the zeroth matrix power. (Show first that, for a class function $f$ and an irreducible representation $\rho$ of
dimension $d$, the matrix $\sum_hf(h)\rho(h)$ is the scalar $\frac1d\sum_hf(h)\chi_\rho(h)$.)
\item Using the character table of $A_5$ (Exercise~\ref{ex:a5}), find the return probability for every $t\ge0$. Show that for $t\ge1$ it simplifies to
\[
\frac1{60}\Bigl(1+16\cdot4^{-t}+25\cdot\Bigl(-\frac15\Bigr)^t\Bigr).
\]
\item Find the probability that after $t\ge0$ turns the icosahedron has turned by a fifth of a turn (in either direction) about some
axis through opposite vertices, and show that the law of the position converges to the uniform law at the rate $4^{-t}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

linear:ex:monotone. Avoid depending on the following exercise.
For any eigenpair Ay=lambda y, choose t=max_i |y_i|/z_i, where Bz=rho_B z.

Find the period and eigenvalues of the directed cycle on $n\ge1$ vertices.
For a connected bipartite graph with at least one edge, put its adjacency
matrix in the form $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

with multiplicities, is symmetric about $0$.
\end{exercise}

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:cycleperiod. A directed n-cycle, n>=1, has period n and
all nth roots of unity, with geometric-coordinate eigenvectors. A connected
undirected bipartite graph with at least one edge has period2: every closed
walk is even and traversing an edge back and forth gives length2.
In a bipartition, A=[[0,B],[B^T,0]], and conjugating by diag(I,-I) gives -A,
so multiplicities are symmetric. Its full spectrum is ±sqrt(mu) for each
positive eigenvalue mu of BB^T, plus p+q-2rank(B) zeros. Earn the finite
Hermitian spectral argument locally if no exact earlier proof is available;
alternatively the characteristic identity X^(q-p)det(X^2 I_p-BB^T), q>=p,
follows by block elimination for X!=0 and polynomial identity. Isolated
one-vertex graph is a necessary exception to the period claim. The original
unspecified graph has no unique numerical eigenvalue list; give the block
description and retain its intended full spectral target. Two stars if this
description is explicitly requested. B: paths2/3, complete bipartite graphs,
unequal part sizes and a single isolated vertex.

entries.hypotheses_domain: 0<=alpha<1; stochastic P and arbitrary probability column v, including zero coordinates.
entries.claim:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{linear:ex:pagerankrate}
Let $0\le\alpha<1$, let $P$ be stochastic, and let $v$ be a probability
column vector, possibly with zero coordinates. Show that every eigenvalue
$\lambda\ne1$ of $G=\alpha P+(1-\alpha)\mathbf1v^{\mathsf T}$ satisfies
$|\lambda|\le\alpha$. Prove that $G$ has a unique stationary probability
row $\pi$, and that $\|\mu G^k-\pi\|_1\le2\alpha^k$ for every probability
row $\mu$ and $k\ge1$, even when $G$ is not irreducible.
\end{exercise}

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:pagerankrate. State 0<=alpha<1 and v>=0, sum v=1.
For every complex row y with y1=0, yG=alpha yP and
||yP||_1<=||y||_1. A left eigenvector for lambda!=1 has y1=0, so
|lambda|<=alpha. The same finite inequality gives contraction on
probability rows: ||mu G^k-nu G^k||_1<=alpha^k||mu-nu||_1.
Existence can be obtained by the Cauchy sequence of iterates, since
successive differences have summable geometric bounds; uniqueness follows
from contraction. For a stationary pi, total variation <=alpha^k and each
coordinate error <=alpha^k. Thus .85^50 is about .000296, not six-digit
accuracy;86 steps guarantee coordinate error below1e-6. B: quotient by
the invariant constants for the eigenvalue bound, direct zero-sum row
recurrence for the error estimate, including alpha=0 and zero entries of v.
Two stars. Eigenvalue moduli alone do not remove Jordan polynomial factors.

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{linear:ex:leslie}
For the Leslie matrix with $n\ge1$, $f_i\ge0$ and $s_i>0$, set $\ell_1=1$.
Show that its characteristic polynomial is $X^n-\sum_if_i\ell_iX^{n-i}$, that it has exactly one
positive root when some $f_i>0$, and that this root is $\rho(L)$, including when $f_n=0$.
Compute a positive right Perron vector, and show that $\rho>1$ if and only
if the \emph{net reproductive rate} $\sum_if_i\ell_i$ exceeds $1$.
\end{exercise}

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:leslie. Take n>=1, s_i>0 and at least one f_i>0,
ell_1=1 and ell_i=product_{j<i}s_j. Expand the first row of XI-L to get
X^n-sum_i f_i ell_i X^(n-i). Let m=max{i:f_i>0}; the first m-by-m block
is irreducible, giving a positive root rho. The Euler–Lotka function
F(t)=sum_i f_i ell_i t^(-i) is strictly decreasing on t>0, so F(t)=1 has
exactly that root. The vector z_i=ell_i rho^(-(i-1)) z_1 is strictly
positive even when f_n=0; a weighted maximum-coordinate argument shows
that every eigenvalue has modulus<=rho. F(1)>1 iff rho>1.
B: use the eigenvector recurrence rather than determinant expansion,
and split the characteristic polynomial into the first m block and
the remaining zero eigenvalues. Include n=1, f_n=0 and all f=0
(the latter is nilpotent and excluded from the positive-root assertion).
Two stars. Convergence in the main application requires x0>=0, x0!=0,
and the stable proportions are z/sum z.

entries.hypotheses_domain: Primitive doubly stochastic n-by-n P; fixed independent random position permutations on d cards.
entries.claim:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{linear:ex:doublystoch}
Let $P$ be an $n\times n$ primitive matrix with both row and column sums $1$
(\emph{doubly stochastic}). Show that $P^k\to J/n$.
A shuffle of $d$ distinct cards chooses a permutation of positions from a fixed
probability distribution, independently of the current deck order and of
earlier choices. Show that its transition matrix on the $d!$ orders is doubly
stochastic. Deduce convergence to the uniform distribution when that matrix
is primitive.
\end{exercise}

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:doublystoch. Column sums1 make the uniform probability
row stationary; primitivity gives uniqueness and convergence to J/n.
For a shuffle, explicitly require a state-independent random permutation
of the d positions: each deterministic position permutation induces a
permutation of all d! orders, hence its matrix is doubly stochastic, as
is their fixed probability mixture. Primitivity then gives the uniform
law on orders. B: invert each position permutation to count exactly one
preimage per destination; do not infer double stochasticity from
primitivity alone. A two-state positive matrix with both rows(3/4,1/4)
is the counterexample to the overly broad wording. Two stars.

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:wielandtsharp. Assume n>=2 and a positive-length walk.
Every departure from1 must first follow1,2,...,n; before its return to1
it may take the n->2 detour any number of times. Concatenating visits
to1 gives length an+b(n-1), a>=1,b>=0. If this equalled(n-1)^2,
reduction modulo n-1 would make a a positive multiple of n-1, forcing
an>=n(n-1)>(n-1)^2. For n=2 the same conclusion says no length1
loop at1. Upper positivity is the proved Wielandt bound, so the exponent
is exactly(n-1)^2+1. B: enumerate Boolean walk supports for small n,
including n2, and independently check the modular obstruction. Three stars.

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:circ3. Write s=a+b+c and Q=a²+b²+c²-ab-bc-ca, so N=sQ.
Modulo3, Q=s², hence3|N forces3|s and3|Q, so9|N. Thus residues±3mod9
are impossible. Conversely N=3m+1 uses(m+1,m,m), N=3m-1 uses(m-1,m,m),
and N=9m uses(m+1,m-1,m), for every integer m, including negatives and0.
B: direct expand all three parameter families; exact residue enumeration
checks necessity. Main example's sign claim is false at a=b=c!=0: N0
but s!=0. State the equality case rather than certify the old assertion.
Two stars retained.
entries.adversarial_check_B: Supplied constructions(3k+1,3k+2,9k) match the independently found(3m+1,3m-1,9m) families after index changes. Mod3 forces both the sum and quadratic factor divisible by3, hence N divisible by9. All729 residues and negative/zero parameter values exact. The main sign error at a=b=c!=0 is corrected, not blamed on this correct answer.

linear:ex:fourier. F²_jk=(1/n)sum_l omega^((j+k)l)=1 if k=-jmodn,
else0. Thus F²=R, R²=I and F4I. Any eigenvalue lambda obeys lambda4=1;
no claim every fourth root occurs for every n. B: act on each Fourier basis
vector and compare reversal. n1/n2 endpoints, no0 denominators because n>=1.
One star.

test nonsymmetric kernels to catch transform signs. Singleton group and
zero functions included. Two stars.

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:walsh. Order word/character pairs by their first bit; its
character factor is(-1)^(x1 t1), giving blocks[[H,H],[H,-H]]. Compute Hf0
and Hf1 recursively, then their sum/difference. T(n)=2T(n-1)+2^n,
T0=0 gives T(n)=n2^n scalar additions/subtractions. B: butterfly order
can instead add/subtract f0/f1 first and apply H to each. H0=[1] and
n0 zero operations. Two stars.
entries.adversarial_check_B: Supplied first-bit character factor gives correct block order. Both butterfly orders compute the same result; recurrence2T(n-1)+2^n,T00 gives n2^n. n0 base is H0=[1]; main now defines tensor/block notation and earns the count before using it.

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:gausssign. For a square a=r², substitution x->r x gives
g(a)=g1. For a nonsquare, aD is the set of nonsquares; since
sum_nonzero zeta^u=-1, 1+2sum_nonsq zeta^u=-g1.
Equivalently g(a)=sum_u eta(u)zeta^(a u)=eta(a)g1 after u->a^-1u,
with eta0=0. Under p=1mod4 and g1>0 the square-indexed eigenvalues
are(-1+sqrt p)/2. B: exact cyclotomic coefficient comparison for each
nonzero a, without numerically choosing a square-root sign. Two stars.
entries.adversarial_check_B: Supplied scaling by square classes plus total sum0 proves nonsquare sign reversal for every odd prime. Independent direct square/nonsquare complement sum or eta-substitution proves it again. Conditional p1mod4,g1>0 eigenvalue assignment retained. Fixed zeta determines the sign; wording no longer suggests it is a free choice.

entries.reconstruction_A:
linear:ex:paleyramsey. Squares mod17 are{1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16}.
Any edge(u,v) maps by x->(x-u)/(v-u) to(0,1), preserving adjacency
because v-u is a square. Common neighbours of0/1 are{2,9,16}; none
are adjacent to each other (differences3 or10 up to sign are nonsquares).
Thus no4-clique exists, while{0,1,2} is a triangle, so clique number3.
Self-complementarity gives independence number3. Colour K17 by Paley
edges/nonedges: no monochromatic K4, hence R(4,4)>=18.
B: enumerate all triples/quadruples exactly and verify both colours.
The sqrt17 bound gives at most4 and does not itself exclude a4-clique.
Define Ramsey number locally; if existence is needed, earn the elementary
R(a,b)<=R(a-1,b)+R(a,b-1) recurrence by splitting a vertex neighbourhood.
Two stars.

Define Ramsey number in prompt; locally earn existence via finite recurrence. No unproved exact R4,4=18 upper bound retained.

\begin{exercise}[$\star$]\label{combinatorial:ex:nearpencil}
For $n\ge3$, check Fisher's inequality is attained with $\lambda=1$ by the
\emph{near-pencil} $\{1,n\},\{2,n\},\dots,\{n-1,n\},\{1,\dots,n-1\}$.
Check the same formula's degenerate cases $n=1,2$ separately.
For a second example, define the \emph{Fano plane} to have points
$\mathbb F_2^3\setminus\{0\}$ and lines $\{u,v,u+v\}$ for distinct nonzero
$u,v$. Show that it has seven lines and that these attain Fisher's bound
on its seven points.
\end{exercise} Exact domains and endpoint checks: Supplied Fano answer already defines/proves the vector-space model; the prompt's future V9 reference was unnecessary and is removed. Every e_i+e_j has coordinate sum2, an
affine hyperplane of dimension n; translate by2/(n+1) times the all-ones
vector and choose an orthonormal basis to identify it isometrically with R^n.
For distinct two-subsets I,J, squared distance is4-2|I intersect J|, hence
2 or4. There are binom(n+1,2) distinct points. For n3, translate by(1/2,...,1/2):
complementary pairs give opposite unit vectors on3 mutually perpendicular
axes, the regular octahedron. B: Gram matrix/difference coordinates and all
six points/15 distances. Need define two-distance as *at most* two values:
n1 gives one point and n2 equilateral triangle has only one distance.
n0 gives no edges/empty set. One star.

entries.hypotheses_domain:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{combinatorial:ex:dvir}
\emph{Dvir's Kakeya theorem.} Let $q$ be a prime power and $n\ge1$.
A set $K\subseteq\mathbb F_q^n$ is a \emph{Kakeya set} if it contains a line in every direction: for every $d\ne0$ there is $x$ with $\{x+td:t\in\mathbb F_q\}\subseteq K$. Show that
$|K|\ge\binom{q+n-1}n$. (Use a non-zero polynomial of degree at most $q-1$ vanishing on $K$, and look at its restriction to lines. Lemma~\ref{combinatorial:lem:grid} holds over any field.)
\end{exercise} Exact domains and endpoint checks: Supplied rank-nullity/top-homogeneous argument is sound in positive dimension and already treats constant degree. Explicit n>=1 now earns K nonempty from a nonzero direction, fixing original n0 counterexample(empty K but claimed lower1). Reconstruct evaluation-map kernel, line root bound, leading coefficient and individual-degree grid lemma separately. Exact plane Kakeya enumeration over F2/F3/F4 gives minima3/7/10, satisfying the respective general bounds3/6/10; n1 full field and q2 covered.
